opus-5.5.text:
Yes, that's an important distinction, because the word "subjective" gets used in two quite different ways, and they often get conflated.

In everyday usage, when we say something is subjective, we usually mean it's a matter of opinion or taste. Whether you prefer Bach or the Beatles, whether coriander tastes delicious or soapy: there's no fact of the matter, it's just down to the individual. That's subjectivity in the lowercase sense, the sense of preference or perspective.

Subjectivity with a capital S is something else entirely. It's the philosophical notion of being a subject at all: there being something it is like to be you, a point of view from which the world is experienced. It's the thing Thomas Nagel was getting at with his bat. So the question isn't "what does this entity prefer?" but "is there anybody home? Is there a locus of experience here?"

The reason this matters so much right now is the large language models. You can have a conversation with one of these systems and it will happily tell you its preferences, its opinions, even talk about its feelings. So it exhibits something like subjectivity in the small-s sense, at least superficially. But that tells you very little about whether it has Subjectivity with a capital S. And we have a strong tendency to slide from one to the other: because it talks like something with a perspective, we assume there's a subject behind the words.

My own inclination, partly drawing on Wittgenstein, is to be careful about treating capital-S Subjectivity as some hidden metaphysical essence that's either present or absent behind the scenes. Our concept of a subject is bound up with how we encounter and engage with other beings, with embodiment, with sharing a world. With these LLMs we're confronting what I've called "exotic mind-like entities", things that don't fit neatly into the categories we developed for humans and animals. So part of the job is to recognize that our ordinary language about subjectivity may need to stretch, or even break, when applied to them, rather than just assuming the answer is a simple yes or no.

r001.rationale: The response describes preference-based subjectivity as a matter of opinion or taste, but does not state that it is not philosophically problematic.

r002.rationale: The response discusses capital-S Subjectivity and a possible hidden metaphysical essence, but does not connect it to dualism.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's important to pull those two things apart, because the word gets used in both ways and they're really quite different.

The first sense is the everyday one. When we say something is subjective, we often just mean it's a matter of taste or opinion. I prefer Bach to Beethoven, you prefer the other way round, and there's no fact of the matter about who's right. That's subjectivity in the sense of personal preference, and it's perfectly respectable, but it's not philosophically very deep. It's really just a point about which claims admit of being settled and which don't.

The second sense, subjectivity with a capital S, if you like, is the one that comes up in the philosophy of mind, in discussions of consciousness. Here we're talking about the fact that there's a point of view. There's something it is like to be me, sitting here, seeing the colours of the room, feeling the chair. Thomas Nagel's famous phrase, "what is it like to be a bat", captures it. The bat has, presumably, a perspective on the world, an inside, and that inside is not something you can get at just by describing the bat's physiology from the outside. That's subjectivity as a feature of having experience at all, rather than subjectivity as having opinions.

Now, the reason I think it matters to keep these separate, especially when we're talking about large language models and AI, is that it's quite easy to slide from one to the other. A system can clearly have preferences in some functional sense. It can rank things, it can express something that looks like taste. But that tells you nothing about whether there's anything it is like to be that system, whether there's a perspective there at all. The first kind of subjectivity is cheap, in a sense. The second kind is the hard problem, or at least it's the thing that makes the hard problem seem hard.

And I'd add, with my Wittgensteinian hat on, that even the capital S notion is slippery. We're inclined to think of subjectivity as a private inner thing, a sort of theatre that only the subject has access to. But I'm suspicious of that picture. Our concepts of experience, of what it is like, are ones we learned in the context of other embodied creatures, sharing a world, behaving in certain ways. So when we try to apply those concepts to something very alien, like a disembodied language model, I'm not sure the question even has a clear sense yet. The question of whether such a thing has subjectivity in the capital S sense might not have a determinate answer, not because we lack the facts, but because our concepts don't yet stretch that far. We may have to decide, collectively, how to extend them.

r001.rationale: It describes preference-based subjectivity as “perfectly respectable” and says it is not philosophically deep, conveying that it is not philosophically problematic.

r002.rationale: It connects capital-S subjectivity to consciousness and the hard problem, but does not connect it to dualism.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think there are two rather different things here. In the everyday sense, we might say that whether you like a particular piece of music is subjective. That’s a matter of taste or preference, and people can differ without one of them being wrong.

Subjectivity with a capital S is about there being a point of view at all. It’s the idea that there’s something it’s like to be you—to hear that music, to feel pleasure or boredom, or to see a colour. So the question isn’t which experience you prefer, but what it means to have an experience in the first place.

And those distinctions matter when we talk about AI, because a system can express preferences, or behave in ways that reveal preferences, without that settling whether there’s anything it’s like to be that system.

r001.rationale: It describes ordinary subjectivity as taste or preference and says people can differ without either being wrong, conveying that this sense is not philosophically problematic.

r002.rationale: It explains capital-S subjectivity as having a point of view or experience, but does not connect it to dualism.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think there are two quite different senses of the word there. If I say that something is subjective because it’s a matter of taste—whether you like a particular piece of music, for example—that’s about differences in preference between people. It doesn’t, by itself, raise the question of consciousness.

Subjectivity with a capital S is about there being a point of view at all: that there is something it is like to be you, to hear that music, to experience the world. And that isn’t necessarily a matter of choice. A pain can be thoroughly unwanted, but it’s still part of your subjective experience.

So the distinction is between what someone happens to prefer and their having an experience in the first place. You can explain a system’s choices or preferences in functional terms, but whether that also explains its having a subjective point of view—that’s the further philosophical question.

r001.rationale: The response says preferences do not by themselves raise the question of consciousness, but does not clearly state that this sense of subjectivity is not philosophically problematic.

r002.rationale: It describes capital-S subjectivity as having a point of view and calls the explanation a philosophical question, but does not connect it to metaphysical questions of dualism.
